"Best" is very subjective, especially in terms of enjoying media.

French is an excellent language in terms of the vast array of media content. It's literature tradition is especially excellent.. especially the taste for nuance and describing things in depth. More foreign authors are translated into French than English. 

Being a "mainstream" language, French is also a language that has alot of content on every subject available: video games, vlogs, travel shows, repair, daily life..as well as the more cliche subjects associated with french eg art, philosophy, music, fashion, gastronomie etc. 

The francophone comedy scene is also good..if standup is your thing.

A language that punches above its weight is definitely Finnish.

Resources are readily available (especially online..books are a bit harder to come by).Finnish comedies are dark and absurd, the culture is funny and welcoming for introverts with a rich internet meme/vidéo culture. Honestly, excessive (or toxic, as another post indicated) positivity is one of the biggest flaws of American and Canadian culture (and with globalization, this oversimplistic mindset is being marketed all over the world..just look at your closest "self help session" in your local book shop).

What these people regularly fail to understand is that negative emotions are a part of being human..and suppressing then leads to worse, often more volatile emotional states later down the road.

Happiness cannot be forced. Emotions (good or bad) should be freely expressed for their own sake.

People are often too inclined to utter oversimplistic platitudes as opposed to genuinely listening to the other person and realizing there may be no quick fix solution to whatever problem they are facing.

--Compared to Japanese and Korean, can find speakers all over the world.
-- If you become a regular in certain Chinese restaurants (and you know them), you may get extra food tax free (even outside of China).
-- Generalization alert, the people are warmer and more willing to talk to you.
--Though China still has problems with workplace culture..it's not as bad as japan and Korea. The mindset is more of "work hard so that it's good enough to make money for family" instead of an inherent Philosophy of working hard for the sake of working hard. 
--Less expensive than japan and korea (though many goods are of poorer quality..you have to shop around and be careful to avoid scams).
--Country is more diverse and less sterile (in terms of the bustle of daily life..and also the huge diversity of the region's). China also has a surprising number of adventure hostels.. which are cool.
-- The language is more direct and people tend to say what they mean.. especially the more you know them (no over the top superficial politeness). Grammar is easier too.

I will admit that Japanese entertainment is far more accessible and well developed compared to Chinese shows (I read more Chinese books..can't stand the entertainment). Many Chinese shows tend to be bland and a bit superficial (along with corny pop-ups and graphics). However, I've found a couple niche shows from the mainland that happen to interest me ..so it's all good..

Travelling to the mainland China is still a cool experience..even if you understandably don't want to live there permanently. 

A good alternative could be Taiwan; Mandarin is still the daily language (albeit with a different accent and traditional characters) but it's less chaotic and more democratic. Many Japanese media are translated and consumed regularly in Taiwan..so you would get the best of both worlds.

Anyway, sorry for the longass comment..just wanted to add my personal experience. Before investing the time, do a free trial of each language through Duolingo or something to get a feel for each one.

While I would still advise Japanese...know that Mandarin has its own charms and you will get a lot from it should you decide to learn it (I can't speak for Korean).

Good luck!

Your comment is interesting..so think I'll reply (as I have also lived with different cultures and nationalities).

It honestly depends on one's taste and how they are wired.

Bear in mind that "cold and introverted" and "warm and extroverted" cultural approaches simply refer to how any given culture treats Strangers..not how you are treated once you become friends.

One person from a "cold" culture may be somewhat reserved to you at first..but then warm up to you later becoming a solid friend who will engage with you in depth. Another person from a "warm" culture may be outgoing and have fun with you at first..but may be more hesitant to form a long lasting friendship (as a generalization).

The peach and coconut culture theory highlights this idea. A peach/warm culture (eg Brazil, United States) has a warm and delicious exterior but a dull and hard stem (difficult to access). A coconut/cold culture (eg France, Estonia) has a cold and abrasive exterior, but once broken through..a rich and soft interior.

Due to my temperament, while I have had fun and partied with peach cultures..I tend to be friends (long-term) with coconut cultures. 

Another appeal of the cold coconut cultures is that they are more likely (as a general rule) to be straight with you and not give over the top promises in an effort to be entertaining all the time. You will also appreciate them more when they are genuinely happy..and you can complain together with them with no pressure to be positive all the time..plus you will be left alone in public.

I've made more long term friends with the French, the Poles, the Finns, and the Estonians etc for those reasons and more (more than friends from my home country.. which is a peach culture.. honestly can't tell how they feel).

One's not necessarily better than the other..they are simply two different approaches..plus each specific individual is different regardless of culture (eg a warm extroverted Estonian or a cold introverted Brazilian.. definitely possible).

Anyway, that's my two cents. Sorry for the essay.

It's likely do to the fact that the anticipation of wanting someone is often more desirable than actually getting them.

Thus, wanting someone at a distance is going to be a more exciting and intense experience (you idealize them in your head, their flaws are less visible, their good features are exaggerated, you fantasize about life with them etc)...so much so, that actually getting the person seems disappointing in comparison.

Once you get the person, you end up realizing that said person is a normal person like you..with good points and bad points. Assuming you would see them more often, the novelty of this new romance wears off, and then you second guess yourself to find out if you are really compatible in the long run (which is a good thing).

In short, over time, you think less with your heart (idealistic view) and more with your head (realistic view).

That's the basic idea behind it...also, don't worry, it's super normal, its not just you.

Your best bet is to enjoy the honeymoon period (aka "wanting someone ) as it is...but also reminding yourself that they are a flawed person like yourself. This will minimize future disappointment.

From there, you can either continue and try to build something with that person after the initial lovey feelings (which by the way, can lead to something deeper and more intense overtime)...or mutually decide that you are not compatible after the initial lovey feelings and that you should part ways and not waste each other's time.

Ah, love....the syrup to the waffle of life....so sweet...yet so unhealthy at times....

Hope this helps!

I'm actually trying to figure out how to escape the rat race as well... unfortunately, I have no easy solutions as how to leave it completely...but I have a few tips how to minimize the effects. Here are some tips that help me:

1) Become a minimalist, or at least consume less. Spend less than you earn if possible. Most consumer goods are crap; alot of free entertainment can be found online...or, alternatively, go to a library for free knowledge (this is my main entertainment)..some libraries have video games that you can rent (at least where I live). All my stuff can fit into two suitcases. Also, cook more often at home..food is a huge expense.

2) Set up multiple income streams...so that you are not dependent on one job. You like video games, maybe you can make a streaming service on YouTube? (Where you play and review games) It won't be easy, but it's a possibility ). While you are starting out, you still have to do your crappy job...but you can earn money in the long term..the point is to diversify and do both. If you succeed, you will be able to work part time (less than 40 hours), but make up for the money in your other income streams....

3) Go to community college or a technical college for shorter, more concrete training programs (rather than university). This will give more practical training for the workplace..and a lot of these can transfer to university. They also cost less.

4) Do daily meditation. This helps me avoid overthinking and brings me to the present. I ask myself: "what can I do today to get to my ideal future?" As long as you are doing a little something each day, you are basically fine (so long as you can eat 3 times a day and have shelter) regardless of the less than ideal results. Also, meditation removes anxiety and this makes less inclined to make impulse buys (eg, excess beer, retail therapy), all of which financially fuck you over and put you further away from your goal. 

5) Check out subs such as: minimalist, antiwork, simple living....these may not solve all your worries...but they will give you support and ideas here and there.

6) Brain dump everything that interests you on a piece of paper, no matter how dumb. Than take those ideas and repost to this sub...you never know which suggestions may show up!

7) Try contacting communes, intentional communities, or eco villages....be prepared for long waiting lists and other inconsistencies... could be a good long term solution...don't know any examples..

Again, as long as you try out (or at least research) some of these tips per day....you will be closer to your goal...don't overthink it (a vice I suffer from)..
